notes.meaning: God commands that the inner gate facing east remain shut throughout the six normal workdays, but open on the Sabbath and at the New Moon. The closed gate set apart ordinary working hours from sacred time. Opening it on holy days welcomed worshippers into God's presence for rest and celebration. Setting aside special times for worship keeps our daily labor in healthy balance.

The prince enters the gateway porch and stands by the post while the priests offer his sacrifices. He bows down in worship at the threshold of the gate and leaves, while the gate stays open until evening. Even though he is the ruler, he does not act as a priest or enter the inner court. True leaders show humility by honoring God's order and worshipping reverently.

The common people must bow down in worship before the Lord at the entrance of this same east gate on Sabbaths and New Moons. They stood in the outer courtyard just behind their leader to offer their prayers. This gathered the whole community together in regular, united praise. God welcomes both rulers and everyday citizens to draw near to him.

On the Sabbath, the prince supplies six healthy lambs and one ram for a burnt offering, which completely belonged to God on the altar. He also provides flour and olive oil, giving a fixed measure of grain with the ram and as much as he is able for the lambs. These amounts were far larger than the older laws required, reflecting abundant joy and generous worship. God loves a willing heart that gives according to what he has provided.

For the monthly New Moon festival, the prince brings a flawless young bull, six lambs, and a ram, paired with grain and oil. As on the Sabbath, he provides set amounts of flour for the larger animals and gives as much for the lambs as his hand can afford. Marking the start of each month kept God's people thankful for the steady gift of time and harvest. Remembering the Lord regularly keeps our gratitude fresh throughout the year.

Whenever the prince comes to worship on these special days, he must enter through the porch of the gateway and leave the same way. This clear rule guided his steps so the sacred areas stayed peaceful and orderly. Having set paths in God's house prevents confusion during sacred services. Order in worship helps everyone keep their focus on the Lord.

During the annual festivals, worshippers entering by the north gate must leave through the south gate, and those entering by the south must leave through the north. No one was allowed to turn around and exit through the door they came in. This one-way traffic kept huge crowds from running into each other in the courtyard. Walking straight ahead through the temple reminded them to keep pressing forward in their walk with God.

At the major festivals, the prince enters the temple together with the crowds and departs when they leave. He does not take a private path or hold himself above the rest of the people. Instead, he joins in the shared worship of the congregation as a fellow servant of God. Good leaders encourage others by standing shoulder to shoulder with them in worship.

God sets the amounts of grain and oil that must accompany the animal offerings at all appointed feasts. Every bull and ram was matched with a full measure of flour and oil, while the gift with the lambs was according to what the giver could give. These standard rules ensured that every festival was properly supplied without putting an unfair strain on anyone. God desires our worship to be thoughtful and well planned.

If the prince decides to bring a freewill offering on a regular day, the east gate is opened for him. He presents his offering just like he does on the Sabbath, but as soon as he leaves, the gate is shut behind him. This showed that God welcomed spontaneous gifts of praise, not just scheduled festival worship. It also preserved the special sacredness of the east gate on ordinary workdays.

Every morning, the temple ministers must offer a year-old lamb, along with flour and olive oil, as a regular burnt offering. Unlike the older law given through Moses, no evening lamb is mentioned here. Starting each morning with an offering showed that the people continually needed God's favor and owed him their daily lives. Giving God the start of our day helps keep our hearts directed toward him.

differ.view: Some evangelicals believe these daily offerings will literally take place in a future earthly kingdom to serve as memorial reminders of Jesus' sacrifice on the cross.
Reformed Christians understand these daily sacrifices as symbolic imagery pointing to Jesus, whose final death on the cross completely ended all animal offerings.

notes.meaning: God states that if the prince gives part of his royal estate to one of his sons, it becomes a permanent family inheritance. Because God gave the prince his own large territory, he had plenty of land to pass down. This rule kept the prince's family well provided for across future generations. Parents have a natural duty to care for their children's future.

If the prince gives land to a servant, that land only belongs to the servant until the year of liberty, also known as the Jubilee. In that fiftieth year, all sold or gifted land went back to its original owner, so the property returned to the prince and his sons. This law prevented the royal family's land from being lost over time. It maintained a clear difference between the lasting rights of a son and the temporary gifts given to a servant.

God strictly forbids the prince from seizing the land of ordinary people or forcing families off their property. Any inheritance he provides for his sons must come entirely from his own royal lands so the people are never scattered. Past kings in Israel had abused their authority by stealing family farms from their subjects. God expects leaders to protect the rights of their people rather than using power to make themselves rich.

The prophet's guide takes him to the holy rooms on the north side reserved for the priests. He points out a cooking area at the far western end where priests boil the guilt offerings and sin offerings, which helped restore fellowship with God, and bake their holy grain offerings. Cooking these items in private prevented the holy food from touching common people in the outer courtyard. God taught his people to treat sacred duties with great care and reverence.

The guide leads Ezekiel into the outer courtyard and shows him four enclosed courts, one in each corner. Every single corner court had the exact same size, measuring forty cubits long and thirty cubits wide. These spaces were separated from the main court to handle practical temple tasks. God pays close attention to detail and creates orderly spaces for his worship.

Inside each of the four corner courts, stone shelves ran along the walls with cooking hearths underneath. These built-in fireplaces provided room to boil large amounts of meat during the major festivals. The temple was thoughtfully designed so that many people could prepare their food at the same time. Practical planning makes it possible for large communities to celebrate together smoothly.

The guide explains that these four corner areas are the kitchens for the Levites who assist at the temple. Here they boiled the peace offerings brought by the worshippers so the people could share a meal. While the priests cooked their own food in private rooms, these outer kitchens served the everyday families. Feasting together in God's presence turned worship into a joyful family and community celebration.
